transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-08
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Reed (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (CTO, Zenith Data), Liam O'Sullivan (Head of Platform), Priya Nair (ML Engineer)
---
[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm maya with redwood inference, i'll kick off. Um, quick intros?
[00:18] Aisha Khan: hi i'm aisha, cto at zenith, we run a data platform for financial reporting, lots of ingestion, and we're evaluating llm infra for summarization and a new chat feature.
[00:30] Liam O'Sullivan: liam here, head of platform, i'll be thinking about cost and infra ops, network/security.
[00:38] Priya Nair: priya, ml eng, building the summarization and embeddings pipeline.
[00:42] Maya Patel: great, jonah from our se team will talk through the economics and technical levers. quick agenda: workloads, current stack, cost targets, tradeoffs hosted vs dedicated vs private, then next steps.
[01:05] Jonah Reed: hey everyone, nice to meet you. quick q to start — what's your current traffic shape (qps, avg token lengths, % real-time vs batch)?
[01:18] Priya Nair: so right now proto traffic is small: peaky during market hours, maybe 30 rps peak for embeddings and 5 rps for generation, avg prompt length for gen is ~400 tokens, responses avg 300 tokens, but summaries can be up to 1k tokens. Batch jobs are large — nightly summarization of 200k docs.
[01:42] Jonah Reed: helpful. And budget or unit economics targets? are you optimizing for lowest latency or lowest cost?
[01:49] Aisha Khan: budget is the big constraint — we can scale spend if outcomes justify it but initial target is under $20k/month for inference. Latency matters for chat — 300-500ms tail is preferred, but we can accept 800ms for complex prompts.
[02:05] Maya Patel: ok that's helpful. quick framing — hosted gives fastest time-to-value, predictable per-use pricing; dedicated gives lower unit cost at commit and better isolation; private has similar economics to dedicated plus infra/OPEX. Jonah, maybe you can sketch typical per-token ranges and levers?
[02:25] Jonah Reed: yeah, so rough numbers to anchor — on a per-1k-token basis, hosted for our curated base models is typically in the low cents range for smaller models and moves higher for larger models — ballpark, think something like $0.02 to $0.12 per 1k tokens depending on model family and size. Dedicated reserved capacity can reduce unit cost by roughly 30–60% depending on commit and batching. Important: those headline numbers are blended; your realized cost depends a lot on batching, KV/prefix caching, and token breakdown (prompt vs completion) — so batching can improve throughput and amortize GPU costs, caching avoids re-sending identical prefixes, and quantization can cut infra cost further for private/dedicated.
[03:22] Priya Nair: can you unpack batching numbers a bit — like if we go from synchronous 1-at-a-time to micro-batching, what delta should we expect?
[03:32] Jonah Reed: sure, in practice micro-batching can yield 1.5x–3x improvements in GPU utilization for typical seq lengths. For example, if your requests are short and you can stack 8-16 requests per batch, your per-token cost goes down because the fixed kernel startup cost is amortized. For long sequences the benefit is less dramatic. Also note latency tradeoffs — batching increases tail latency if you wait to fill batch. Hosted has smart queuing that tries to balance latency SLOs.
[03:58] Liam O'Sullivan: what about caching — we have a lot of repeated prefixes in our summarization pipeline (same boilerplate, templates). How much can caching actually save?
[04:08] Jonah Reed: prefix/KV caching helps a lot for repeated contexts — you can see 30–70% token savings depending on how much of your prompt is boilerplate. For highly templated prompts caching is huge. Redwood supports automatic prefix caching for dedicated/private with shared cache across workers; hosted also supports caching but policies differ.
[04:35] Aisha Khan: earlier you mentioned quantization — what's the practical unit delta there?
[04:42] Jonah Reed: quantization affects GPU memory and throughput. Moving to 8-bit-ish variants often allows more batch concurrency per GPU and can reduce infra cost by 10–40% depending on workload and model compatibility. It's more of a dedicated/private play often since you control kernels and quantized builds, but we also offer quantified model variants in hosted catalog.
[05:06] Maya Patel: quick real-talk on economics — the difference between hosted and dedicated often looks like a per-token premium for hosted convenience plus autoscaling costs. If you have steady load that justifies reserved capacity, dedicated tends to have better unit economics.
[05:23] Priya Nair: for our nightly batch, would dedicated be strongly preferred?
[05:27] Jonah Reed: for large nightly jobs, dedicated or private is usually more cost effective because you can run large batches, tune quantization, and avoid per-request overhead. Hosted is great for the interactive chat piece while you're ramping. Many customers do hybrid: host chat on Redwood hosted, run heavy batch on dedicated or private. We route requests by policy.
[05:49] Liam O'Sullivan: can you share an example blended calculation? like if we do 1M tokens/month mixed?
[05:56] Jonah Reed: quick back-of-envelope: assume a blended hosted rate of $0.05 per 1k tokens (this is example only). 1M tokens => 1,000 * $0.05 = $50. Wait, that math — to be precise, 1M tokens is 1000 * 1k tokens, so at $0.05/1k it's $50. But typical production workloads are tens to hundreds of millions of tokens; if you're at 100M tokens and hosted $0.05/1k => $5,000. With dedicated that might drop 40% to $3,000 equivalent. The point being you should run a pilot with representative prompts to get accurate blended numbers.
[06:42] Aisha Khan: those example numbers help. Our concern is unpredictable spikes during market events — can dedicated handle bursts or do we need burst capacity?
[06:52] Jonah Reed: dedicated supports burst capacity and autoscaling policies; you can configure reserved base capacity plus burst into shared pool or hosted fallback. That's a common pattern for trading off cost and availability.
[07:05] Priya Nair: on the security side, for private deployment, how does key management/audit logs work?
[07:11] Maya Patel: we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for private, SAML/SSO and role-based access; audit logs are available in the console and can be exported to SIEM. We'll send SOC2 docs in the follow-up.
[07:26] Liam O'Sullivan: for the benchmark you proposed, what config do you need from us?
[07:31] Jonah Reed: a representative prompt set (Priya mentioned that), traffic pattern (qps distribution), preferred models, and success criteria: cost per 1k tokens target, tail latency SLOs. We'll run a mixed workload benchmark (chat + summarization + embeddings) of 10k–50k requests. We'll show breakdowns: tokens by prompt/response, batching configs, caching hit rates, and estimated monthly run-rate cost.
[07:57] Aisha Khan: our initial acceptance criteria: below $20k/mo, chat tail p95 <800ms, summary throughput for nightly job <4 hours. Does that sound reasonable?
[08:07] Maya Patel: yes, that's a good start and we can iterate.
[08:12] Jonah Reed: quick note on embeddings — they're a different unit, billed per vector or per request depending on provider; embeddings are usually much cheaper per call but can dominate cost if you generate millions of vectors. We'll include embedding cost in the benchmark.
[08:28] Priya Nair: question — can caching be shared between hosted and dedicated or is it isolated?
[08:35] Jonah Reed: cache scope is configurable; for customers using both hosted and dedicated we typically keep caches separate for tenant boundaries, but you can use a shared cache approach for private deployments. We'll document tradeoffs, but security considerations often push separate caches.
[08:52] Maya Patel: i'm going to share a simple worked example in the follow-up pricing sheet — showing token mix, batching assumptions, caching hit-rate, and resulting unit cost.
[08:58] Liam O'Sullivan: when you say "40% savings on dedicated", is that purely from reserved instance discounts or also from batching gains?
[09:05] Jonah Reed: it's blended — reserved capacity discounts give you lower $/GPU-hour, and batching/quantization increase effective throughput per GPU, so both contribute. The exact split depends on workload.
[09:18] Aisha Khan: any gotchas for latencies with batching and caching in a live chat? we need sub-second.
[09:25] Jonah Reed: for sub-second you usually rely on small micro-batches (or single-request fast paths) and aggressive cache hits. Hosted supports low-latency lanes and you can pin a warm pool for chat routes. P95 goals under 500–800ms are achievable for common models with that configuration.
[09:42] Priya Nair: let's talk numbers for a realistic pilot — for 10k mixed requests in pilot, what will you measure and how long does it take to run?
[09:51] Jonah Reed: we'll run at realistic concurrency to mimic your peaks; it might take a few hours depending on sequences. We'll return a report with per-route token counts, cache hit rate, batching distribution, latency percentiles, and extrapolated monthly cost at different scale points.
[10:10] Aisha Khan: ok, from a procurement perspective, what's the contract footprint for dedicated — monthly commit, cancellation terms?
[10:18] Maya Patel: dedicated can be monthly or annual commitments; annual gives best rates. We can be flexible on proof-of-concept month-to-month. We'll outline options in the pricing packet.
[10:27] Liam O'Sullivan: security checklist — do you support private link / VPC peering and customer managed keys?
[10:33] Maya Patel: yes on VPC peering and private link for private deployments; KMS integration is available for private and dedicated with proper controls.
[10:42] Priya Nair: any performance difference between hosted and dedicated for same model binary?
[10:46] Jonah Reed: negligible at the model kernel level if running equivalent hardware and quantization, but dedicated gives you control to tune kernels, batch sizes, and memory layouts; hosted has optimized defaults but less low-level tweakability. In practice dedicated often achieves better throughput because you can push higher concurrency and batch sizes.
[11:05] Aisha Khan: what about multi-region latency for our EU customers?
[11:10] Maya Patel: Redwood offers multi-region routing; you can pin routes to region, and we can replicate caches to region to reduce cold-starts. There's cross-region cost and replication tradeoffs we'll show.
[11:22] Liam O'Sullivan: do you have a recommended rollout strategy for hybrid model (hosted chat + dedicated batch)?
[11:29] Jonah Reed: start with hosted for chat to get product feedback, spin up small dedicated pool for nightly jobs and run pilot benchmarks; once you have steady throughput, increase commit to dedicated and migrate batch workloads, then evaluate migrating chat to dedicated if the numbers justify it. Use canary routes during transition.
[11:50] Priya Nair: quick question — does Redwood show token-level cost breakdown per request in the console?
[11:56] Maya Patel: yes, the console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and exportable reports for billing.
[12:04] Aisha Khan: about quotas — can we set hard budget caps to prevent runaway costs?
[12:09] Maya Patel: yes, you can set budget alerts and hard limits per-project or per-route. We'll show examples in the pricing doc.
[12:17] Liam O'Sullivan: can we get a sample of a customers' benchmark report? even anonymized?
[12:22] Jonah Reed: yes we can provide anonymized case studies and a sample benchmark report.
[12:28] Aisha Khan: one more — embeddings storage costs, do you handle vector DBs or is that separate?
[12:34] Priya Nair: (interject) we plan to use an existing vectordb vendor.
[12:37] Jonah Reed: Redwood doesn't host vectordb by default but we integrate with common vendors; embedding costs are separate and we'll estimate them; ops for storing millions of vectors is part of the overall cost discussion.
[12:52] Maya Patel: ok, i want to recap and make sure we captured the ask — pilot with representative prompt set, target <$20k/mo at steady state, tail p95 for chat <800ms, nightly summarization <4 hrs, provide promps/traffic from your side. we'll send pricing/security docs.
[13:10] Aisha Khan: yep that sums it up. One small nit — when you said per-1k tokens numbers earlier, can you clarify what counts as "tokens"? does our tokenizer align with your billing?
[13:20] Jonah Reed: good point — we bill on model tokenization, which usually aligns with common tokenizers (bpe-like). We'll run your prompts through the tokenizer in the benchmark so you see exact counts and billing.
[13:34] Liam O'Sullivan: for the pilot, is there any charge for Redwood to run the benchmark?
[13:39] Maya Patel: we usually include a free benchmark run for qualified prospects; we will use it to size recommendation and will show expected costs if you ran same workload in production.
[13:49] Priya Nair: ok great. can we also test quantized variants?
[13:53] Jonah Reed: yes, we'll include quantized builds when available and show throughput/latency tradeoffs.
[14:00] Aisha Khan: any other customer references specifically on cost reductions?
[14:04] Maya Patel: we can share anonymized case studies showing customers achieving 30–60% unit cost reductions by moving batch to dedicated and leveraging caching + quantization.
[14:15] Liam O'Sullivan: timeline — how soon can we get the pricing sheet and schedule the benchmark?
[14:21] Maya Patel: i'll send pricing and security docs by Friday 2025-10-10. Jonah will follow up to schedule the benchmark once we get the prompt/traffic data.
[14:30] Aisha Khan: sounds good.
[14:33] (small side chatter about calendar invites and timezones)
[14:45] Priya Nair: i'll share the prompt set by sunday and include tokenization examples.
[14:50] Jonah Reed: perfect, we'll prepare the benchmark harness and the reporting template.
[15:00] Maya Patel: ok final quick note — for cost modeling it's useful to see 3 scenarios: conservative (no caching/batching), expected (some caching, micro-batching), and optimized (high caching, dedicated, quantized). We'll include that in the sheet.
[15:20] Aisha Khan: great, thank you all.
[15:25] Maya Patel: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with docs and next-step scheduling.
---
End of call.
